chunks: High-side NFET advantages and challenges. The question: What are the advantages of using a high-side NFET? What additional challenges are presented?
A high-side switch sits between the supply and the load. An N-channel FET (NFET) is the better switch: lower resistance and cost than a P-channel one of the same size.
The catch: an NFET turns on when its gate (control pin) is a few volts above its source (the pin current leaves by).
On the high side the source is the output, which rises to the supply when the FET is on. So the gate needs a voltage above the supply.
Picture a person who must stay 10 meters above a platform that rises with the water level. When the platform is at 24 meters, the person must be at 34 meters.
A ladder fixed to the ground tops out at 24 and never gets them there. You need a ladder that rides up with the platform.
The riding ladder costs parts, board area and limits on how long the switch can stay on.
The gate must sit 10 volts above the source whenever the FET is on. When the source is at 24 volts the gate is at 34 volts, above the supply rail.
Drive from ground-referenced logic and the high side never turns on.
Gate-source voltage ( V GS ): the gate voltage measured against the source, not against ground. On-resistance ( R DS(on) ): the resistance of the FET when it is on.
Lower means less heat. Bootstrap: a capacitor charged at low voltage, then lifted with the source to give the gate its extra voltage.
Switch node: the output point between the high-side and low-side switches. Charge pump: a small circuit that makes a voltage above the supply, so the FET can stay on indefinitely.
Take a 24 volts supply and an NFET that needs 10 volts of V GS to be fully on. When it conducts, its source is at 24 volts, so the gate must be at 24 plus 10 equals 34 volts.
A 10 volts ground-referenced driver gives V GS equals 10 minus 24 equals -14 volts, so the FET stays off. The payoff: at 10 amps a 10 milliohms NFET wastes 10 squared times 0.
01 equals 1 watts, while a 25 milliohms P-channel FET wastes 2. 5 watts. That is the whole idea.
"An NFET is the better switch because electrons are two to three times more mobile than holes, so for the same die it has lower on-resistance and gate charge, and it's cheaper with more choices.
The challenge on the high side is that its source is the switch node, so the gate has to be a few volts above the supply, which needs a floating gate supply: a bootstrap capacitor or charge pump.
That limits duty cycle and complicates start-up, and adds undershoot and dv/dt issues."
